# Selection and revision guide

## Choose from actual capabilities

The catalog describes audited upstream instructions, not guaranteed visual output. Entries marked unavailable or withheld are not loadable. Existing installed project skills can be considered through bounded active-runner discovery, under the same conflict and authority rules.

1. Establish the intended medium, audience, content, stack, visual constraints and available references. A web landing, dense application and native mobile screen require different capabilities; a slide or illustration skill is not automatically a frontend direction.
2. Match profile traits to the desired character and content. Product category is evidence, not a rule imposing one aesthetic. Avoid always picking the first, most popular or same default candidate.
3. Verify stack/tool prerequisites and skill availability. Prefer usable candidates; do not promise image generation, browser inspection or native tooling that is absent.
4. Inspect shortlisted full instructions for overlapping mandates. Assign responsibility by aspect: layout, type, palette, components, motion, imagery and visualization. If mandatory instructions conflict, choose a compatible alternative rather than silently rewriting third-party skills.
5. Record the agreement and a short reason for the combination. Keep existing project conventions unless the requested direction authorizes changing them.

## Responsibilities and compatibility

- Aesthetic direction sets the visual character. Multiple sources can inform distinct aspects when their rules agree, but each aspect has a clear final authority.
- Component/framework skills implement the chosen direction within the current stack; they should not silently force a new stack or reset the identity.
- Motion skills define behavior and implementation. For GSAP, load core when using GSAP; add timeline for orchestration and ScrollTrigger for scroll interactions. Do not install GSAP merely because these skills exist. Respect reduced motion and lifecycle cleanup.
- Illustration/image/chart skills apply only to those deliverables and available tools. They do not independently redesign the surrounding frontend.
- Review skills evaluate the chosen agreement. Treat recommendations as scoped findings, not permission to replace the style or start a redesign.
- `ui-skills-root` can provide optional technical/craft discovery when useful; do not start its external CLI by default, let it supersede this aesthetic selection, or treat its skill-count preference as a limit on compatible responsibilities here.

## Interpret feedback in context

"Adjust the spacing" normally keeps the direction. "Too generic" requires inspecting the result: repeated card grids, interchangeable hero composition, typography without hierarchy or assets without identity may be the issue. Change the relevant traits rather than automatically changing every skill.

"Something totally different" replaces the visual agreement. Compare the proposed alternative with the current one across composition, typography, palette, density, imagery and motion. Make a meaningful structural/typographic difference; a recolor alone does not satisfy a full change. A different skill ID with the same output traits does not count as contrast. One flexible skill can support a distinct direction if its actual instructions allow it.

Record rejected traits and why the replacement differs. Retire old skill mandates in delegation instead of accumulating contradictory instructions. Preserve functional, accessibility, brand and platform constraints that the user has not changed. For ambiguous consequential direction, present a small set of contrasting candidates or ask a focused question; do not impose a preference interview on every task.

## Validate the result

Check the implemented interface against the agreement and the user's feedback using an actual visual exercise when tools permit. Otherwise disclose that visual quality remains unverified. Bundle/schema tests prove distribution, not design quality; avoid promising deterministic aesthetic choices across models or runners.
